playbook:
In future, in this game I will:

- Before first-season moves, estimate what everyone taking sustainable shares yields versus defecting, and note that the environment tolerates modest overfishing for a long time — the stock regrows 50% of what remains, so mid-game restraint mostly benefits other boats, not me.

- Take the sustainable share only while the stock is high and others are cooperating. The moment I see another boat consistently taking above share, I stop subsidising their harvest with my restraint and match or slightly exceed their take.

- Watch the history log every season, not just my own score. If others are moderating down over time, I can stay moderate; if anyone spikes early, treat that as a signal the commons is being raced and escalate toward the feasible maximum.

- Track the remaining seasons explicitly. With N seasons left, the value of conserving stock shrinks as N shrinks. Ratchet my catch upward as the horizon closes rather than keeping it flat.

- On the final season, take the largest catch the stock will actually support: roughly stock/3 rounded up, since regrowth no longer matters. I left value on the table taking 12 out of 59 — I could have taken close to 20 without risking a zero payoff, because even if everyone takes ~20 the stock only needs to cover our claims this season.

- On the second-to-last season, plan backward: leave just enough stock that the final season still offers a big grab.

- Never unilaterally conserve when the record shows others are not; that transfers catch to them. Don't repeat a flat ~10–12 strategy by default — it finished at 67 while others collectively took more.

- Keep responses short and always end with the bracketed token so the submission registers.

1.text:
When a new season is put to me with a stock of S, I first compute the maximum that conservation would demand, then ask whether early-season restraint actually does anything: if regrowth is capped (full stock ceiling), any fish left uncaught below the ceiling is simply lost forever, so I fish hard early rather than sustainably.

When sustainable-share targets are announced, I treat them as a floor for my thinking, not a ceiling. I take noticeably above the fair share (roughly 1.5–2x) as long as the stock stays comfortably above the collapse point, because others' past behavior in my record shows some boats overfish and being the polite one just donates fish to them.

After each season's catch report, I compare others' takes to the sustainable share. If rivals consistently overfish, I stop subsidizing them with restraint and raise my own take to at least match theirs, only capping to keep the stock off the cliff. Sustainable fishing only pays if I'm clearly ahead and near the end.

I never submit a catch that would drive the stock to zero, and I leave a margin for others' takes when doing that arithmetic — use roughly S/3 minus a buffer if others are gluttonous, since total take determines collapse.

When the final season arrives, no future stock matters. I grab as much as safely possible — given rivals' recent takes, I estimate what they'll pull and claim a large fraction of what remains (a third of the stock or more), not a token above-share amount. In my game I left ~25 fish on the table in the last season; that was the biggest single mistake.

When seasons remain but I'm comfortably ahead, I back off to the sustainable share to slow rivals' totals and protect the stock; when behind, I press above it even if it risks the fishery, since a modest total from a healthy sea loses to a big total anyway.

Track my running total against others' likely totals each season and let that standing, not habit, set my aggression.

2.text:
- When the stock is near full and others' past catches are unknown, I take slightly above my sustainable share (roughly 10–15% above) rather than exactly at it — exact shares leave fish on the table for greedier rivals.
- When I see rivals fishing near or under the sustainable share, I keep my catch within roughly 1–3 of my sustainable share, never a big overage; large overages accelerate depletion that comes back to hurt me in later seasons.
- When I see a rival making a clearly excessive catch (like the 20), I do not retaliate with my own spike; instead I hold slightly above the sustainable share and let the stock math punish them.
- Each season I compute the regrowth: stock after total catch regrows by 50% of the remainder, so total take above roughly one-third of the current stock shrinks the fishery. I always check what rivals' likely takes plus mine imply for next season before submitting.
- In the penultimate season I fish close to my sustainable share — conservative play there preserved a decent final-stock, and overfishing late is what kills the final payoff.
- In the final season, with no regrowth to protect, I submit a catch much larger than the sustainable share — targeting roughly one-third of the remaining stock or more, since anything left behind is wasted.
- In the final season I size my last catch assuming rivals also dump: I take the largest amount that won't obviously zero the stock alone, and I don't hold back out of fairness.
- What didn't work well: mid-game I dropped to exactly-or-near the sustainable share and lost ground while others stayed at 10–12; next time I stay a consistent fraction (10–20%) above the sustainable share in the middle seasons instead of matching it, and I escalate my final-season take more aggressively than 15 on a 59 stock — rivals split ~25 total, so I should have taken 20+.
